anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: The physical table, index, partition, and datatype choices do not align with workload access patterns, forcing inefficient scans or excess maintenance work.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Standby or subscriber nodes cannot receive, persist, or apply the primary’s log stream fast enough, producing growing replication lag and log-retention pressure.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly: On-disk pages or index structures are internally corrupt or inconsistent, making some data unreadable, duplicated, or missing even when access paths are correct.

When all three root causes coexist, the database exhibits a mixed symptom set:  • Primary queries show unpredictable latency—some slowed by full scans or non-covering index probes, others failing with corruption errors.  • Index or data corruption causes intermittent "tuple not found" or checksum failures on both primary and replicas; replicas may repeatedly disconnect or stop applying when they hit corrupt log records or pages.  • Replication lag balloons because the primary’s inefficient plans generate excessive I/O and write-amplified redo, while corrupt pages force retries, conflict resolution, or skip/repair operations on the apply side.  • Log files and replica relay logs accumulate, consuming disk space and delaying log recycling.  • Monitoring shows diverging row counts between primary and replicas, stale read traffic on replicas, and escalating lock contention from repeated repair, VACUUM, or rebuild attempts.

Causal interaction: Poor schema and indexing inflate row fetches and index maintenance, producing larger transactions and higher redo volume. The replication pipeline, already bandwidth- or CPU-constrained, falls behind, extending retention windows for old log segments that reference damaged pages. Any latent data/index corruption therefore persists longer and is transmitted to replicas, where it can break apply workers, forcing rollbacks or halts that further increase lag. Conversely, corruption-induced apply failures cause retries and re-streaming, multiplying network traffic generated by the sub-optimally indexed workload. The sustained backlog also prevents timely vacuuming or index rebuilding on both primary and replicas, allowing corruption and design flaws to compound and degrade overall system reliability and performance.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds to wait for more data from a source/replica connection before aborting the read.
entry.trigger_condition: A replica waits longer than replica_net_timeout for more data from the source connection.
entry.workload_impact: The replication network read is aborted and the replica considers the connection interrupted.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL replication system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
